title: Fannie Lou Hamer
hook: a sharecropper beaten for registering voters sings This Little Light of Mine

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mountaintop, and Moses seeing a land he wouldn't enter. Your line: look toward the promised land.

A bus full of tired people is rolling back from a county courthouse in Mississippi. They've just tried to register to vote, and been turned away. Police stop the bus on a made-up charge. Fear goes through the seats like a draft. Then one woman, a sharecropper who spent long years in the cotton fields, starts to sing. A church song. Others join in. That woman is Fannie Lou Hamer. That evening the plantation owner tells her to take back her registration or leave. She leaves.

Hamer grew up in the Mississippi Delta, in a family of sharecroppers, and she grew up in church. When young organizers came asking Black citizens to register to vote, she raised her hand. It cost her the home and the work she had, and later more. Coming back from a voter workshop, she and others were arrested in the town of Winona, and in that jail she was beaten so badly she carried the injuries for life. She didn't stop. She sang. Her song was This Little Light of Mine, a gospel song sung in Black churches, and she sang it on buses, in mass meetings, outside courthouses, and, people remember, in jail. It echoes Jesus in the Sermon on the Mount. In the King James Bible: "Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid." And: "Neither do men light a candle, and put it under a bushel, but on a candlestick; and it giveth light unto all that are in the house." A bushel was a basket for measuring grain. Nobody lights a lamp and puts a basket over it. Hamer's little light wasn't small in the end. She told her story to a committee of a national political convention, on television, and asked out loud whether this was the country it claimed to be. She's remembered for saying she was tired of being tired. She also spoke plainly of loving the people who hurt her, because her faith asked it. A small light, in her life, meant one voice that would not go back under the basket.

Hum This Little Light of Mine, or any song about light, or sing one line under your breath; if singing isn't for you, light a candle or a lamp and watch it a while. Notice how a small flame fills a dark room, and think of one good thing you've kept under a basket. If you pray, hold Jesus's words: ye are the light of the world.
Winona, the Mississippi town where she was arrested and beaten so badly she carried the injuries for life, after trying to register to vote.
Your line: this little light. Out from under the basket, and giving light. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Black churches in the United States sing This Little Light of Mine in worship, and it was sung at mass meetings and marches of the civil rights movement.

chat.says: Fannie Lou Hamer was beaten in jail. Why did she keep singing church songs?
options: Her faith said not to hide your light under a basket, so she kept her voice out in the open.
Singing helped her keep quiet about what happened, so nobody would ask her about it.
She sang to show she'd forgiven everyone, so the voting fight could finally be dropped.
chat.meaning: This Little Light of Mine echoes Jesus: ye are the light of the world, not hidden under a bushel. Hamer's voice wouldn't go back under the basket.
